title: Understanding Packages, Functions, and the Tidyverse Workflow
text:
Welcome back to R-Tide!
In our first post, we explored what R is and why it matters. Now it’s time to get hands-on with the tools that make R so powerful. We’ll cover three essential topics:

title: Understanding Packages, Functions, and the Tidyverse Workflow
text:
📦 What Are Packages?
R comes with a set of built-in functions, but its real strength lies in packages — collections of code, documentation, and data created by the community. Think of them as free apps you can install to add new capabilities to R.

Installing and Loading Packages
To use a package, you need to install it once, then load it each session:

# Install the package (do this once)
install.packages("tidyverse")

# Load the package (do this every session)
library(tidyverse)



Common R Packages
Here are some of the most widely used packages, organized by what they do:

📊 Data Manipulation







Package
What It Does




dplyr
The go-to package for data manipulation — filtering, summarizing, arranging, and joining datasets


tidyr
Tools for reshaping data into tidy formats using pivot_longer() and pivot_wider()


stringr
Makes working with text data (strings) easy and consistent


lubridate
Simplifies working with dates and times


data.table
An alternative for very fast operations on large datasets





📈 Data Visualization







Package
What It Does




ggplot2
R’s famous package for creating beautiful graphics using the “grammar of graphics”


plotly
Creates interactive, web-based visualizations


htmlwidgets
A framework for building JavaScript-based visualizations in R





📥 Data Import







Package
What It Does




readr
Fast and friendly way to read CSV, TSV, and other rectangular data


haven
Reads data from SAS, SPSS, and Stata files


DBI
The standard interface for connecting R to databases





📝 Reporting & Communication







Package
What It Does

Create interactive web apps directly from R


rmarkdown

🔧 Modeling & Machine Learning

title: Understanding Packages, Functions, and the Tidyverse Workflow
text:
🔧 Understanding Functions in R
A function is a defined set of code statements organized together to perform a specific task (R Core Team, 2026). Functions are designed to accept inputs, do something with them, and return a useful output (Wickham, 2019).

Three Types of Functions in R
Functions in R come from different sources. Understanding the distinction will help you become a more confident R user:

1. 📦 Package Functions — Verbs from Libraries
These are functions that come with packages you install and load. You need to load the package before you can use its functions.
Example: dplyr verbs

# Load the tidyverse package to access dplyr functions
library(tidyverse)

# filter() - Keep rows that meet conditions
filtered_data <- data |>
  filter(age > 18)

# summarize() - Collapse data into summary statistics
summary_data <- data |>
  summarize(mean_value = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE))

# mutate() - Create new variables
data_with_new_col <- data |>
  mutate(new_column = value * 2)

# arrange() - Sort your data
sorted_data <- data |>
  arrange(desc(value))

# select() - Choose specific columns
selected_cols <- data |>
  select(name, age, value)

Key Point: You must load the package with library(package_name) before using its functions, or use the package::function() syntax:

# Load the package first
library(dplyr)
filtered_data <- filter(data, age > 18)

# OR use the package name directly (no need to load)
filtered_data <- dplyr::filter(data, age > 18)



2. ⚙️ Base R Functions — Built into R
These functions come with R itself. You don’t need to install or load anything extra to use them. They’re always available.

# mean() - Calculate the average
mean_value <- mean(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5))

# sum() - Add up values
total <- sum(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5))

# length() - Count elements
num_elements <- length(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5))

# summary() - Get summary statistics
summary(mtcars$mpg)

# head() - View first few rows
head(mtcars)

# str() - View structure of an object
str(mtcars)

# c() - Combine values into a vector
my_vector <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)

# paste() - Combine text strings
greeting <- paste("Hello", "World")

# read.csv() - Read a CSV file
data <- read.csv("my_file.csv")



3. 🛠️ Custom Functions — Write Your Own
When you find yourself repeating the same code over and over, it’s time to write your own function. Custom functions let you:

Don’t Repeat Yourself (DRY) — Write code once, use it many times
Make code more readable — Give your function a clear name
Easier to update — Change code in one place, not everywhere
Build your own toolkit — Create functions for your specific needs

The Anatomy of a Custom Function:

function_name <- function(argument1, argument2, ...) {
  # Code that does something with the arguments
  result <- argument1 + argument2
  return(result)
}

Example: A simple custom function

# Define a function that calculates the mean and returns a message
mean_with_message <- function(x) {
  mean_value <- mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  message <- paste("The mean is:", mean_value)
  return(message)
}

# Use the function
mean_with_message(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5))

title: Understanding Packages, Functions, and the Tidyverse Workflow
text:
The Tidyverse Workflow
The tidyverse is an opinionated collection of R packages designed for data science that share a common philosophy and grammar. It was created by Hadley Wickham and others to make data science in R more consistent and intuitive.

The Data Science Cycle
The tidyverse is built around a clear, iterative workflow that takes you from raw data to insights. Here’s the cycle:



Breaking Down Each Step

1. 📥 Import
Get your data into R. This might mean reading a CSV file, connecting to a database, or importing from Excel.
Functions used: read_csv(), read_excel(), dbConnect()


2. 📐 Tidy
Transform your data into a consistent structure known as tidy data, where: - Each variable is a column - Each observation is a row - Each type of observational unit is a table
Functions used: pivot_longer(), pivot_wider(), separate(), unite()
As Hadley Wickham famously said: “Tidy datasets are all alike, but every messy dataset is messy in its own way”.


3. 🔄 Transform
Manipulate your data to make it useful for analysis. This is where dplyr shines with its verb functions:



Function
What It Does




filter()
Keep rows based on conditions


select()
Choose specific columns


mutate()
Create new variables


summarize()
Collapse data into summary statistics


arrange()
Sort your data


group_by()
Group data for grouped operations


rename()
Rename columns



Example using dplyr verbs:

# Chain dplyr verbs together with the pipe
data |>
  filter(age > 18) |>                    # filter() - keep adults
  select(name, age, income) |>           # select() - choose columns
  mutate(income_thousands = income / 1000) |>  # mutate() - create new column
  group_by(age_group) |>                 # group_by() - group data
  summarize(mean_income = mean(income))  # summarize() - collapse data



4. 👁️ Visualize
Create plots to explore your data and communicate findings using ggplot2.
Functions used: ggplot(), geom_point(), geom_bar(), geom_histogram(), geom_boxplot()


5. 📊 Model
Build statistical models to capture signals in your data.
Functions used: lm(), glm(), train(), rand_forest()


6. 📝 Communicate
Share your results using tools like R Markdown or Quarto.
Functions used: Quarto markdown, code chunks, inline R code



The Iterative Cycle
A key insight from this workflow is that it’s not a straight line — it’s a cycle:
           Import
             ↑
    Communicate → Tidy
             ↓
       Model ← Transform
             ↓
         Visualize
You might: - Visualize your data, notice something interesting, then go back to transform it further - Build a model, visualize the results, then communicate your findings - Import new data, tidy it, and continue the cycle


The Pipe Operator: %>% or |>
One of the tidyverse’s signature features is the pipe operator, which allows you to write code in a clear, step-by-step style:

data |>
  filter(condition) |>
  group_by(category) |>
  summarize(mean_value = mean(value))

Each step takes the result from the previous step and passes it along, making your code read like a recipe.

title: Understanding Packages, Functions, and the Tidyverse Workflow
text:
🎯 Putting It All Together
Here’s how the tidyverse workflow might look in practice:

# 1. Import the data
library(tidyverse)
data <- read_csv("survey_data.csv")

# 2. Tidy - reshape if needed
data_tidy <- data |>
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("q"), 
               names_to = "question", 
               values_to = "response")

# 3. Transform - clean and summarize
data_clean <- data_tidy |>
  filter(age > 18) |>
  mutate(age_group = case_when(
    age < 30 ~ "18-29",
    age < 50 ~ "30-49",
    TRUE ~ "50+"
  ))

# 4. Visualize
data_clean |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age_group, y = response)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#2A9D8F")

# 5. Model (linear model example)
model <- lm(response ~ age_group, data = data_clean)

# 6. Communicate results in a Quarto document

title: Welcome to R-Tide
text:
The Story Behind R-Tide
R-Tide started with a simple observation: keeping up with R is hard to do alone.
Not because the community isn’t sharing—it’s sharing constantly. Blogs, tweets, LinkedIn posts, conference talks, package releases, YouTube tutorials. It’s a firehose of amazing content.
The problem isn’t a lack of information. It’s that information isn’t the same as learning.
Learning happens through conversation, experimentation, and shared experience. It happens when someone explains a concept differently, demonstrates a workflow, or asks a question that sparks a new way of thinking.
R-Tide was created to be that space. A place where we don’t simply collect links, but build understanding together.

The tide is predictable, powerful, gains strength through momentum, and lifts everything in its path. That’s exactly what we want R-Tide to be for the R community—a rising wave that carries all of us forward, together.



Stay curious. Stay connected. Ride the tide together.
— The R-Tide Community
(Starting with one person—you—and growing with every new member who joins the tide)

title: What is R? A Beginner’s Introduction
text: Welcome to R-Tide! If you’re new to R, or just curious about what makes it so special, this post is for you. We’ll explore what R is, where it came from, how it evolved, and where you can start your learning journey.

title: What is R? A Beginner’s Introduction
text:
A Beginner’s Introduction
R is a language and environment for statistical computing and graphics (R Core Team, 2026). At its heart, R is designed for people who work with data, whether that’s analyzing survey results, building predictive models, or creating publication-quality visualizations.
But R is more than just a programming language. The R Project describes it as an “environment”—a fully planned and coherent system for data manipulation, calculation, and graphical display. This environment includes:

Effective data handling and storage
Tools for calculations on arrays and matrices
A large collection of intermediate tools for data analysis
Graphical facilities for display on-screen or in print
A programming language with conditionals, loops, and user-defined functions

One of R’s greatest strengths is its extensibility. Users can add new functionality by defining functions or installing packages—collections of code, documentation, and data created by the community. Today, thousands of packages are available through CRAN (the Comprehensive R Archive Network), covering everything from machine learning to bioinformatics.
R is also free and open-source. It’s a GNU project, available under the GNU General Public License, which means anyone can download, use, and modify it without cost (GNU Project, 2026).

title: What is R? A Beginner’s Introduction
text:
A Brief History of R
R’s story begins with another language: S. S was developed at Bell Laboratories in the 1970s and 1980s by John Chambers and colleagues as a tool for statistical computing (Chambers, 1998). It was designed by statisticians—not computer scientists—to link together calls to trusted FORTRAN packages.
R was created in 1993 by Ross Ihaka and Robert Gentleman at the University of Auckland, New Zealand (Ihaka & Gentleman, 1996). The name “R” is a playful nod to both its creators’ first names and its relationship to the S language.
The project was conceived in 1992, with an initial version released in 1995 and a stable beta version in 2000 (R Core Team, 2026). R became an official part of the GNU Project in December 1997 (GNU Project, 2026).
While R’s syntax resembles S, its underlying implementation is actually derived from Scheme, a dialect of Lisp (Ihaka & Gentleman, 1996). The developers first wrote an interpreter for a Scheme subset and then progressively modified it to resemble S.
Key milestones in R’s development include:



Year
Milestone




1993
R is first created by Ihaka and Gentleman


1995
Initial version released


1997
R becomes an official GNU Project; CRAN launched


2000
Version 1.0 released—considered stable for production


2004
Version 2.0 introduced lazy loading


2013
Version 3.0 released



Today, R is developed by the R Development Core Team and supported by the R Foundation for Statistical Computing.

title: What is R? A Beginner’s Introduction
text:
From RStudio to Posit
If you’ve been around R for a while, you’ve probably heard of RStudio—the popular integrated development environment (IDE) that made working with R much easier.
RStudio was founded by J.J. Allaire in 2009 as an open-source project, with Joe Cheng joining soon after to help develop the Shiny web framework in 2012. Over the years, the company brought on key contributors including Hadley Wickham (creator of ggplot2 and the tidyverse), Garrett Grolemund (creator of lubridate), and Yihui Xie (creator of knitr and R Markdown).
In 2020, RStudio became a Public Benefit Corporation (PBC) , codifying its open-source mission into its corporate charter and balancing the interests of community, customers, employees, and shareholders (Posit PBC, 2025).
In July 2022, the company announced a name change to Posit PBC. This wasn’t a move away from R—in fact, as Chief Scientist Hadley Wickham put it, “I’m not going to stop writing R code” (Wickham, 2022). Rather, the name change reflected the company’s broadening focus to support other programming languages like Python, making it a “single home for R & Python” data science.
Today, Posit continues to lead contributions to over 250 open-source projects, with the RStudio IDE remaining the premier environment for R development.

title: What is R? A Beginner’s Introduction
text:
What is R Used For?
R is incredibly versatile. Here are some of its most common use cases:
Data Science & Machine Learning
R is a go-to language for predictive modeling, clustering, classification, and AI applications. Libraries like caret, randomForest, and xgboost make it easy to develop machine learning models.
Statistical Analysis & Research
R is extensively used in academia, scientific research, and economics for hypothesis testing, regression analysis, and survey data interpretation.
Data Visualization
Organizations use R to generate interactive dashboards, charts, and reports with packages like ggplot2, shiny, and plotly.
Healthcare & Bioinformatics
R plays a crucial role in genomics, drug discovery, and epidemiology through the Bioconductor package.
Finance & Quantitative Trading
R is used in financial modeling, risk analysis, and algorithmic trading with packages like quantmod and TTR.
Government & Policy Analysis
Government agencies use R for census data analysis, public health research, and social science modeling.

title: What is R? A Beginner’s Introduction
text:
Resources for Beginners
Starting with R can feel daunting, but there are many excellent (and free!) resources to help you learn:

📖 Online Textbooks & Guides

R for Data Science (2nd edition) by Hadley Wickham and Garrett Grolemund — A free online book that introduces you to R, RStudio, and the tidyverse (Wickham & Grolemund, 2023).
YaRrr! The Pirate’s Guide to R — A clear, free online textbook for beginners (Phillips, 2025).
R-Tutor.com — A well-structured guide with examples (R-Tutor, 2026).



🎓 Free Online Courses

Software Carpentry: R for Reproducible Scientific Analysis — An introduction to R for people with no programming background (Software Carpentry, 2026).
RStudio’s Online Learning Guide — Extensive links to learning resources from getting started to interactive Shiny apps (Posit PBC, 2025).



🖥️ Learning Inside R

Swirl — An R package that teaches you R interactively directly in the R console. Just run install.packages("swirl") to get started (Swirl, 2026).



🛠️ Getting Started

Download R from cran.r-project.org
Download RStudio (now Posit) from posit.co
Follow a beginner tutorial from the resources above
